strengths: The manuscript presents an understandable, modular system comprising controller-based expert routing, cross-modal memory, interruption handling, and parallel TTS. Explicit control tokens and workflows make its behavior more inspectable than a monolithic end-to-end model. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/d2de93f17ae3447fb24f0dd86f160dfa/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The proposed training-free integration paradigm is practically useful: expert models and modalities can in principle be replaced or extended without retraining the complete system.

The evaluation covers numerous image, video, OCR, mathematical, and diagram-understanding benchmarks. The reported Video-MME improvements after adding ASR are potentially valuable, especially for long videos where audio information is complementary.

The paper supplies an architecture diagram, pseudocode, controller prompt, control-token protocol, memory schema, and TTS segmentation rules, giving a reasonably clear high-level account of the intended system.
weaknesses: Soundness is the decisive weakness. The paper does not specify which experts are invoked for each benchmark item, how their outputs are combined, or what produces the reported score for “Ours.” Comparisons between a system that can select among multiple large experts and individual fixed models do not isolate the benefit of orchestration. Essential controls—same experts without the controller, fixed or oracle routing, single-best-expert performance, and routing/fusion ablations—are absent.

The central component claims are not empirically substantiated. Static benchmark scores cannot support the claim that cross-modal memory improves context-aware tasks, and there is no multi-turn memory benchmark, retrieval evaluation, compression-fidelity study, or memory ablation. Likewise, interruption handling, full-duplex interaction, extensibility, and interpretability are asserted but not systematically evaluated.

The video gains appear to come from supplying ASR transcripts to vision/video models, which changes their input information rather than cleanly testing the proposed controller. The manuscript provides insufficient protocol detail to determine whether base and orchestrated variants receive equivalent information or whether benchmark audio/transcripts are used fairly.

The TTS evidence is inadequate. The 10.3% improvement compares 0.204 s with 0.183 s without identifying the TTS model, hardware, text set, sample count, timing definition, or uncertainty. Claims of maintained voice quality, natural rhythm, and seamless concatenation have no objective metric or human listening study. Moreover, the complete system remains slower than GPT-4o in Table 1 (3.2 s versus 1.2 s), so the broader efficiency framing is misleading.

Reproducibility is poor: there is no code or artifact link; no complete expert registry, routing logs, decoding parameters, benchmark prompts, evaluator versions, hardware, model/API versions, cost accounting, repeated-trial statistics, or per-cell result provenance. The statement that some results come from official papers does not identify which entries, leaving unclear whether evaluation conditions are comparable.

Originality is limited. LLM tool routing, structured conversational memory, and chunked/streaming parallel TTS are established system patterns. The paper surveys related agent systems but does not sharply demonstrate a technical distinction, algorithmic advance, or new understanding beyond combining these components.

Presentation is visually readable but technically imprecise. Several equations are largely restatements of the pipeline rather than operational definitions; sequence decomposition is written as a set union; retrieval, fusion, compression, prosodic adjustment, and runtime semantic classification remain underspecified. Numerous grammatical and typographical issues further obscure implementation details.

The manuscript contains no meaningful limitations, ethics, or risk discussion. A continuously listening system that stores visual and audio information raises privacy, consent, retention, security, and misuse concerns; representing data as an “encrypted_blob” in a schema is not an evaluated safeguard. Bias and failure propagation across routed experts are also unaddressed.

Overall, the architecture is a plausible engineering prototype, but unsupported attribution of benchmark gains, missing ablations, and insufficient reproducibility prevent reliable validation of its central scientific claims. Substantial new controlled experiments and implementation disclosure are needed before acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and important systems problem: combining specialized multimodal models without retraining. The modular controller/expert design could make systems easier to update and inspect than an end-to-end model.

The control-token interface, structured cross-modal memory, interruption handling, and segmented TTS pipeline form a coherent high-level architecture. The worked interaction example makes the intended behavior understandable.

The evaluation attempts broad coverage, including image, video, OCR, mathematical reasoning, diagrams, and speech latency. The reported Video-MME gains from adding ASR suggest that inference-time modality composition can be useful, particularly for long videos.

The manuscript is generally organized around clearly stated components, and the explicit routing decisions could provide better operational interpretability than latent routing inside a jointly trained model.
weaknesses: Soundness is the decisive problem. It is unclear what exact system produces each reported score: the paper lists numerous 7B/32B/72B and proprietary experts but does not report per-benchmark routing, selection criteria, call counts, prompts, or whether expert selection uses benchmark/task identity. Consequently, the results could reflect choosing stronger models or an implicit ensemble rather than the proposed orchestration mechanism.

The comparisons do not control resources or information. A controller plus several experts, including models as large as Qwen2.5-VL-72B and Qwen-VL-Max, is compared against individual models without matched parameter count, inference compute, API use, latency, or monetary cost. The claim of significantly reduced computational resources is therefore unsupported.

Benchmark methodology is insufficient for verification. The manuscript omits dataset versions, evaluation toolkit and scoring settings, prompts, preprocessing, decoding parameters, number of runs, uncertainty, and contamination safeguards. It also states that some baseline numbers were copied from official papers, making the table a mixture of potentially incompatible evaluation settings.

There are no controlled ablations for the central claims. The paper does not compare learned/prompted routing against a fixed router, oracle router, strongest single expert, random routing, or simple task-specific dispatch. It likewise provides no ablations of memory retrieval, memory compression, ASR fusion, or the controller. In particular, Finding 2 attributes performance to cross-modal memory despite presenting no memory intervention or long-context evaluation.

Several reported results are internally unclear or inconsistent. Table 1 reports 65.58 on Video-MME, whereas Figure 3 reports orchestrated scores of 71.9 and 76.4 for two configurations without reconciling them. The text alternates between Qwen2-VL and Qwen2.5-VL, and incorrectly presents MMMU as temporal reasoning. These issues further weaken confidence in the headline improvements.

The method is mostly a specification of familiar components rather than a reproducible algorithm. The retrieval functions, modality integration, runtime semantic classifier, compression policy, expert registry, failure handling, and prosodic concatenation are left abstract. The appendix supplies only a small prompt, pseudocode, a JSON schema, and elementary segmentation rules; no code, executable configuration, model checkpoints, or artifact link is provided.

The TTS evidence does not support the claimed full-duplex, natural-speech system. The paper gives no TTS model, hardware, sample size, workload, timing definition, statistical test, or units for the per-character metric. A roughly 21 ms mean reduction is reported without end-to-end latency or time-to-first-audio measurements. Claims about voice quality, prosody, seamless interruption, and stability lack objective audio metrics or human evaluation.

Originality is limited. LLM tool routing, structured conversational memory, ASR-assisted video inference, and parallel synthesis of text chunks are established systems patterns. Their integration may be useful engineering, but the manuscript does not identify or experimentally validate a sufficiently distinct technical insight over existing agent orchestration frameworks.

Presentation quality is below the expected standard: there are frequent grammar and spacing errors, vague promotional claims, underdefined notation, and Figure 4 is visibly clipped at the right edge. The paper also lacks a substantive limitations section.

Research ethics and deployment risks are not addressed. A system retaining raw multimodal inputs, embeddings, dialogue history, and allegedly encrypted blobs raises privacy, consent, retention, and security questions, yet encryption and data governance are unspecified. The paper also omits discussion of expert-model hallucinations, harmful routing failures, proprietary-service dependencies, and the environmental or financial cost of invoking multiple large models. strengths: The manuscript presents a practically appealing, modular system that combines controller-based routing, cross-modal memory, specialist models, interruption handling, and parallel TTS without additional end-to-end training. The complete manuscript was reviewed here: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/b323387293064e45869f49d32fd0afaf/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
The system-level perspective is useful and potentially significant: replaceable expert modules could make multimodal assistants easier to extend and maintain than monolithic jointly trained models.
The explicit control tokens and orchestration workflow make high-level system decisions more inspectable than opaque feature-level fusion.

The reported benchmark results are broad, spanning general vision-language understanding, video, OCR, diagrams, and mathematical reasoning. The reported Video-MME gains are particularly promising for long videos.
The paper supplies pseudocode, a controller prompt, instruction tokens, a memory schema, and TTS segmentation rules, which provide a useful conceptual overview.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central superiority claim is not established by a controlled comparison. The proposed system can select among several expert models, including 7B, 32B, 72B, and commercial systems, but it is compared mainly with individual models. The paper neither fixes an equivalent compute/API budget nor compares against simple ensemble, confidence-routing, or always-use-the-strongest-expert baselines. Consequently, gains such as 88.54 on MMBench and 70.04 on MMMU cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed controller, memory, or orchestration design.

The evaluation lacks component ablations. There are no results removing the controller, memory retrieval/compression, ASR augmentation, specialist selection, or dynamic prompt composer. Finding 2 attributes improvements to cross-modal memory without presenting a memory-specific experiment, while the video gains may simply result from adding ASR transcripts unavailable to the stated base models.

Experimental comparability is unclear because the paper states that some results are copied from official papers. It does not document benchmark versions, evaluation prompts and judging procedures, input resolutions or frame sampling, decoding settings, expert chosen for each example, rerun versus cited results, or uncertainty across trials. Some reported comparisons may therefore use materially different protocols.

The interaction claims are substantially under-evaluated. Full-duplex behavior, interruption handling, routing accuracy, long-session memory retention, and perceived conversational quality receive no user study or quantitative evaluation. Interpretability and extensibility are asserted from the architecture rather than measured.

The TTS study omits the TTS model, hardware, corpus, number and length distribution of utterances, timing definition, number of repetitions, and statistical uncertainty. Processing time falls only from 0.204 s to 0.183 s, while the stronger claims about natural prosody and consistent voice quality have no listening test or objective quality metric. Independent synthesis of chunks could itself harm boundary prosody.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript claims comprehensive open-sourcing but gives no anonymous repository or artifact. The dynamic semantic classifier, retrieval functions, fusion operation, memory prioritization/compression, expert registry, runtime orchestration, and prosodic concatenation remain underspecified; the appendix mostly provides interfaces rather than implementable algorithms.

Presentation needs substantial revision. Notation is sometimes inconsistent or informal, the stated problem maps every request only to audio despite broader multimodal claims, and numerous spacing/grammar errors impede reading. Figure 4 is visibly clipped beyond the page boundary, including part of its legend and right-hand plots.

Originality is moderate rather than high: LLM tool routing, structured conversational memory, and parallel/streaming TTS are established ideas. Their combination is useful engineering, but the manuscript does not clearly distinguish its technical advances from prior multimodal-agent orchestration and streaming pipelines.

Limitations and ethics are not treated adequately. There is no limitations section and no analysis of routing failures, error propagation, hallucinations, latency/cost scaling, privacy of stored audio/images and embeddings, third-party API data exposure, security of tool invocation, or misuse. The JSON schema labels data as an encrypted blob but specifies no threat model or protection mechanism. These omissions are material for an interactive system that persistently stores multimodal user data.
